segments.title: McKinney's Cotton Pickers, Don Redman, and muzak dates
segments.summary: Jones doesn't know the McKinney family and talks about McKinney's Cotton Pickers and commercial muzak dates.

segments.chapter: Early bands and the road to New York
segments.title: Lucky Thompson as a musician and person
segments.summary: Jones calls Thompson one of the greatest musicians he ever knew, with Wardell Gray from the Carew band, and recalls his hardships.

segments.chapter: Early bands and the road to New York
segments.title: Getting the Hot Lips Page job via Cleveland and Buffalo
segments.summary: Lucky Thompson wrote that Page needed a pianist; Jones worked in Cleveland and Buffalo and joined Page at the Onyx Club after a union transfer wait.

segments.chapter: Early bands and the road to New York
segments.title: Buffalo: the Anchor Bar trio without drums
segments.summary: A drumless trio with George Clark helped Jones develop his left hand.

segments.chapter: Early bands and the road to New York
segments.title: Cleveland's Cedar Gardens and meeting Joe Williams
segments.summary: Four or five months at Cedar Gardens, where he met singer Joe Williams; how George Clark came to call him.

segments.chapter: Early bands and the road to New York
segments.title: Hearing Art Tatum in Buffalo and befriending him in New York
segments.summary: Jones heard Tatum three times in Buffalo and later took the near-blind Tatum to work in New York.

segments.chapter: Early bands and the road to New York
segments.title: Big Nick Nicholas and a short-lived Pontiac band
segments.summary: Jones recalls a brief band with Big Nick, a snowstorm drive from Grand Rapids, and Nick's entertainer style compared with Lucky.

segments.chapter: Early bands and the road to New York
segments.title: Edward Bolton and Sonny Stitt
segments.summary: Jones thinks Bolton was Sonny Stitt's father; Stitt never worked in those bands; a taped message from Stitt.

segments.chapter: Hartwick and the CBS staff years
segments.title: Swing Journal and the Japanese promotion machine
segments.summary: The Japanese magazine's coverage and how the recent trip was all promotion, with David Finck on bass.

segments.chapter: Hartwick and the CBS staff years
segments.title: Why Jones moved to Hartwick, New York
segments.summary: Hank and Teddy found the farm while driving on days off from CBS, and he once planned to be a gentleman farmer.

segments.chapter: Hartwick and the CBS staff years
segments.title: Entering the New York recording studio scene
segments.summary: The union six-month transfer rule delayed studio work; a friend recommended him to contractors.

segments.chapter: Hartwick and the CBS staff years
segments.title: Getting the CBS staff job through Andy Williams
segments.summary: Network staffs hired musicians; Jones got CBS in 1958-59 via summer shows with Andy Williams; conductors Ray Bloch and Erwin Cossel.

segments.chapter: Hartwick and the CBS staff years
segments.title: A typical CBS week: rehearsals, tapings and the shows he covered
segments.summary: The routine of rehearsal, run-through and dress rehearsal for the Garry Moore show, later the Gleason and Sullivan shows.

segments.chapter: Hartwick and the CBS staff years
segments.title: The CBS radio Dixieland show
segments.summary: Jones played a Dixieland radio show with staff players and guests like Pee Wee Russell and Jack Teagarden, learning the style by ear.

segments.chapter: Hartwick and the CBS staff years
segments.title: The 'modern jazz' radio show and CBS studios
segments.summary: A staff-based straight-ahead jazz radio show with Hal McKusick and Jimmy Nottingham, recorded in CBS radio studios, often without charts.

segments.chapter: Hartwick and the CBS staff years
segments.title: Working with Jackie Gleason
segments.summary: Gleason was a jazz fan involved in every aspect of the production, and invited Jones to play golf.

segments.chapter: Hartwick and the CBS staff years
segments.title: The Today Show at NBC
segments.summary: Jones played a few times on the Today Show with a small group, before CBS.

segments.chapter: Hartwick and the CBS staff years
segments.title: Tape two: length of the studio years and the end of staff orchestras
segments.summary: Jones was in network studio work nearly twenty years until the staffs were discontinued and the shows moved to California.

segments.chapter: Hartwick and the CBS staff years
segments.title: The closed circle of New York studio musicians
segments.summary: A select group of three or four hundred musicians did most of the work, fewer than a third jazz players; staff names including Specs Powell.

segments.chapter: Hartwick and the CBS staff years
segments.title: Staff pay, benefits and why the jobs were desirable
segments.summary: Staff pay was about $250 a week, less than freelance work; the appeal was steadiness and fringe benefits.

segments.chapter: Hartwick and the CBS staff years
segments.title: His workload: auditions and the Arthur Godfrey show
segments.summary: Jones spent a five-day week on shows, TV casting auditions and Godfrey rehearsals.

segments.chapter: Hartwick and the CBS staff years
segments.title: African-American musicians on network staffs and the race barrier
segments.summary: Very few black musicians were on staff; Jones saw no real barrier and recalls Mingus and Roland Kirk picketing CBS.

segments.chapter: Hartwick and the CBS staff years
segments.title: Balancing staff work with recording dates
segments.summary: Studio schedule left little sleep when recording dates came in; Milt Hinton and Bob Haggard's work.

segments.chapter: Hartwick and the CBS staff years
segments.title: Board of Governors of the Academy of Television Arts
segments.summary: Jones joined in 1964 on a recommendation, found the meetings more social than productive, and left in 1971.

segments.chapter: Piano influences and recording concepts
segments.title: Duke Ellington's influence on Jones
segments.summary: Jones knew Ellington mostly from records and admires his ballads and blues.

segments.chapter: Piano influences and recording concepts
segments.title: Big bands at the Greystone Ballroom and Wall Lake Casino
segments.summary: He heard Earl Hines, Armstrong and Basie in Detroit-area ballrooms in the late 1930s-40s.

segments.chapter: Piano influences and recording concepts
segments.title: Earl Hines and single-line versus two-handed piano
segments.summary: Jones knew Hines from records and heard him in Flint; Hines's trumpet-style lines foreshadowed bebop, unlike the two-handed Waller and Tatum.

segments.chapter: Piano influences and recording concepts
segments.title: The Fats Waller album and Abbey Lincoln, via Jean-Philippe Allard
segments.summary: Allard of French Verve put together the Waller project and 'Bug Waltz' with Abbey Lincoln as well as the Haden spirituals CD.

segments.chapter: Piano influences and recording concepts
segments.title: Producers, concepts and having a 'point of view' on records
segments.summary: Jones values producers as idea men; recording projects work best with a theme and ideas usually come from the producer.

segments.chapter: Piano influences and recording concepts
segments.title: Discovering Fats Waller on records; Nat Cole in Pontiac
segments.summary: Few players came through Pontiac; Jones knew Waller only from records, admiring his rhythm and joy.

segments.chapter: Piano influences and recording concepts
segments.title: Teddy Wilson versus Art Tatum
segments.summary: Wilson was an idol with a pearl-like touch; Tatum was unmatched harmonically and technically, and Jones saw Wilson in Canada.

segments.chapter: Piano influences and recording concepts
segments.title: Clyde Hart, Bud Powell and Tatum's compositions
segments.summary: Hart's harmonic ideas, Powell's single-line style and his tune 'Hallucinations', and Tatum rarely composing.

segments.chapter: Piano influences and recording concepts
segments.title: Merging swing and bebop; responding to drummers' energy
segments.summary: Jones agrees he combines two-handed piano with modern lines and adjusts to drummers like Tony Williams and Elvin.

segments.chapter: Piano influences and recording concepts
segments.title: Break and a joke
segments.summary: A recording stop followed by banter and a psychiatrist joke.

segments.chapter: Piano influences and recording concepts
segments.title: Is there a 'Detroit sound' among pianists?
segments.summary: The interviewer cites a book on a Detroit pianists' sound; Jones says he was never conscious of being its exponent.

segments.chapter: Piano influences and recording concepts
segments.title: Travel, culture and becoming the sum of one's experiences
segments.summary: Jones says a traveling musician absorbs languages and cultures and that his style is the sum of what he has absorbed, never copying note for note.

segments.chapter: Piano influences and recording concepts
segments.title: Not going to college; self-education through reading and seminars
segments.summary: Jones would have chosen the University of Michigan; he now gives seminars and has educated himself by reading.

segments.chapter: Piano influences and recording concepts
segments.title: Self-improvement as a lifelong aim, tied to religion
segments.summary: Jones believes people are here to improve themselves and do good works, a view tied to Christianity.

segments.chapter: 52nd Street, JATP, Savoy and pianos
segments.title: Arriving in New York with Hot Lips Page and playing boogie-woogie
segments.summary: Jones joined Page's blues-based band at the Onyx Club, billed as the kid from the West who played boogie-woogie.

segments.chapter: 52nd Street, JATP, Savoy and pianos
segments.title: 52nd Street clubs and the working night at the Onyx
segments.summary: The row of clubs on Swing Street, a defense of Dixieland, and the Onyx schedule of 45-minute sets from about 9 to 1:30.

segments.chapter: 52nd Street, JATP, Savoy and pianos
segments.title: Don Byas sitting in and Lucky Thompson's saxophone
segments.summary: Byas played forty choruses of 'Sweet Georgia Brown' with Page's band; Jones prefers Lucky Thompson's playing.

segments.chapter: 52nd Street, JATP, Savoy and pianos
segments.title: Playing with Andy Kirk, a gentleman
segments.summary: Jones played theater dates in Andy Kirk's later band and admired his character more than he learned musically.

segments.chapter: 52nd Street, JATP, Savoy and pianos
segments.title: Billy Eckstine's band at the Cotton Club and Fats Navarro falling through the stage
segments.summary: A single engagement with Eckstine's band; Jones tells how Navarro jumped from the top tier and fell through the floor.

segments.chapter: 52nd Street, JATP, Savoy and pianos
segments.title: A couple of months with John Kirby's band
segments.summary: Jones briefly played in Kirby's small band, praising Charlie Shavers's writing and the band's big sound.

segments.chapter: 52nd Street, JATP, Savoy and pianos
segments.title: Joining Jazz at the Philharmonic and recording with Charlie Parker
segments.summary: Norman Granz hired him in 1947 for tours with Hawkins, Lester Young and Parker; a Parker 'Cherokee' studio date in which the drummer had to leave.

segments.chapter: 52nd Street, JATP, Savoy and pianos
segments.title: The 1949 JATP Carnegie Hall recording
segments.summary: The interviewer cites a live Carnegie Hall recording Jones didn't know had been made.

segments.chapter: 52nd Street, JATP, Savoy and pianos
segments.title: Leaving JATP over its circus atmosphere
segments.summary: After about four and a half years, Jones left JATP because showmanship overtook the music.

segments.chapter: 52nd Street, JATP, Savoy and pianos
segments.title: Charlie Parker: calm presence, an offer to join his band
segments.summary: Jones remembers Parker as quiet and businesslike, declined his invitation to join his band, and discusses 'Relaxing at Camarillo'.

segments.chapter: 52nd Street, JATP, Savoy and pianos
segments.title: Accompanying Ella Fitzgerald
segments.summary: Jones worked with Ella for about four years from JATP; she liked full orchestral chords rather than single-line fills.

segments.chapter: 52nd Street, JATP, Savoy and pianos
segments.title: Lessons from accompanying: knowing what to leave out
segments.summary: Accompanying taught him what not to play; Erroll Garner said it took twenty years to learn what to leave out, and Jones criticizes extraneous notes.

segments.chapter: 52nd Street, JATP, Savoy and pianos
segments.title: Savoy sessions in Rudy Van Gelder's Hackensack home
segments.summary: The interviewer lists 1946-47 Savoy dates with Getz, Dizzy Gillespie and J.J. Johnson; Jones says most were in Van Gelder's home.

segments.chapter: 52nd Street, JATP, Savoy and pianos
segments.title: How Jones began recording for Savoy; a discography puzzle and Stan Getz's lost charts
segments.summary: Jones cannot recall his first Savoy date; they puzzle over a Howard McGhee date, and he recalls Getz leaving charts in a taxi.

segments.chapter: 52nd Street, JATP, Savoy and pianos
segments.title: Rudy Van Gelder and his Steinway B
segments.summary: Van Gelder was fiercely protective of his piano, which was the finest Jones ever played; he preferred the home studio sound.

segments.chapter: 52nd Street, JATP, Savoy and pianos
segments.title: Why Jones prefers Steinway pianos
segments.summary: Jones values Steinway's action and tone over Yamaha and other makes.

segments.chapter: 52nd Street, JATP, Savoy and pianos
segments.title: Piano personalities and choosing matched pianos with John Lewis
segments.summary: Every piano sounds different; Jones and John Lewis tried 50 Steinways to find two that matched for their duo record.

segments.chapter: 52nd Street, JATP, Savoy and pianos
segments.title: Attachment to Steinways from JATP and contract requirements
segments.summary: The JATP tours made him a Steinway player; his contract asks only for a tuned, regulated piano.

segments.chapter: 52nd Street, JATP, Savoy and pianos
segments.title: The Ray Brown trio with Charlie Smith
segments.summary: After a doorbell break, Jones recalls Ray Brown's 1948 trio with left-handed drummer Charlie Smith and a photograph of them.

segments.chapter: 52nd Street, JATP, Savoy and pianos
segments.title: Mary Lou Williams's Harlem apartment
segments.summary: Jones visited her apartment once, never knew her well, and calls her a fine pianist and composer.

segments.chapter: 52nd Street, JATP, Savoy and pianos
segments.title: Herman Lubinsky of Savoy
segments.summary: Asked about Savoy's owner, Jones declines to comment.

segments.chapter: 52nd Street, JATP, Savoy and pianos
segments.title: The relaxed Cannonball Adderley session with Miles Davis
segments.summary: Jones recalls the 1958 date with Miles, Sam Jones and Art Blakey as the most relaxed he ever did, on Van Gelder's piano.

segments.chapter: 52nd Street, JATP, Savoy and pianos
segments.title: Cannonball Adderley and Sonny Stitt compared to Charlie Parker
segments.summary: Jones compares Cannonball's earthier playing with Stitt, whom he found the most Parker-like.

segments.chapter: 52nd Street, JATP, Savoy and pianos
segments.title: Bebop versus hard bop
segments.summary: Jones sees little difference between the terms, possibly tempo or line smoothness.

segments.chapter: 52nd Street, JATP, Savoy and pianos
segments.title: Not the Savoy house pianist; why Van Gelder's studio drew everyone
segments.summary: Jones says the Savoy dates were a cycle, and that engineers draw artists; Van Gelder recorded for Blue Note, Prestige and others.

segments.chapter: 1950s clubs, Savoy dates and the Detroit sound
segments.title: Kenny Clarke and Shadow Wilson as drummers
segments.summary: Jones worked at Minton's with Shadow Wilson and praises Kenny Clarke's light touch and brush mastery.

segments.chapter: 1950s clubs, Savoy dates and the Detroit sound
segments.title: Artie Shaw's New Gramercy Five and his perfectionism
segments.summary: Jones recorded with Shaw's small group, doing sixteen to eighteen takes through the night.

segments.chapter: 1950s clubs, Savoy dates and the Detroit sound
segments.title: Shaw compared with Goodman; Goodman borrows Jones's coat
segments.summary: Shaw was the technician and more mature, while Goodman swung harder; the story of Goodman keeping Jones's new coat in Alaska.

segments.chapter: 1950s clubs, Savoy dates and the Detroit sound
segments.title: The Shaw group's personnel and 'horizontal lines'
segments.summary: Players in the small group and Shaw's preference for level, horizontal lines over vertical ones.

segments.chapter: 1950s clubs, Savoy dates and the Detroit sound
segments.title: The Embers: David O. Selznick, Shaw's marriages and his perfectionism
segments.summary: Shaw refused Selznick's request for 'Stardust', married nine times, and perfected recordings more than Goodman.

segments.chapter: 1950s clubs, Savoy dates and the Detroit sound
segments.title: Dating the Shaw gig, and Tyree Glenn at the Roundtable
segments.summary: Shaw used the same library at every job; Jones also worked The Roundtable with Tyree Glenn, Lester Young and Joe Jones.

segments.chapter: 1950s clubs, Savoy dates and the Detroit sound
segments.title: Tyree Glenn's showmanship and private parties in Connecticut
segments.summary: Glenn's vibes and trombone, society parties, and the more structured Dick Gibson jazz parties.

segments.chapter: 1950s clubs, Savoy dates and the Detroit sound
segments.title: Babs Gonzales turning up uninvited in Europe
segments.summary: Gonzales would appear unannounced at festivals such as Nice; Jones calls his book unprintable.

segments.chapter: 1950s clubs, Savoy dates and the Detroit sound
segments.title: A forgotten Savoy date with Lenny Hambro
segments.summary: The interviewer cites a 1953 Savoy date; Jones recalls little of it.

segments.chapter: 1950s clubs, Savoy dates and the Detroit sound
segments.title: Reading through the 1955 run of Savoy dates
segments.summary: The interviewer reads off dates with Clarke, Wendell Marshall, Cannonball, Nat Adderley and others, showing why Jones seemed the house pianist.

segments.chapter: 1950s clubs, Savoy dates and the Detroit sound
segments.title: 'Opus de Funk' played in four keys at once
segments.summary: On a Milt Jackson date Jones had the group play a Horace Silver blues in four different keys at the same time.

segments.chapter: 1950s clubs, Savoy dates and the Detroit sound
segments.title: More 1955 sessions, Marlene VerPlanck, and the unforgettable piano
segments.summary: Date after date, a vocal session, a solo album, and again Jones recalls the Van Gelder piano.

segments.chapter: 1950s clubs, Savoy dates and the Detroit sound
segments.title: Recording with Milt Jackson; a Japanese collector of 550 albums
segments.summary: Jones can't remember all his dates; a Japanese fan collects 550 albums he made, and he recalls Bags and Alvin Jackson.

segments.chapter: 1950s clubs, Savoy dates and the Detroit sound
segments.title: Why so many Detroit musicians recorded in the late 1940s and 1950s
segments.summary: Jones has no explanation for the outpouring of Detroit talent and thinks the 'Detroit sound' was a writer's phrase.

segments.chapter: Marriage to Teddie and family
segments.title: Session three: opening with Teddie Jones present
segments.summary: A recording stop and Satin Doll CD remark; the interviewer opens session three on the evening of Nov 27 with Hank and Teddie Jones.

segments.chapter: Marriage to Teddie and family
segments.title: Teddie Jones on marriage and how she met Hank at Wells' Chicken and Waffle
segments.summary: Teddie describes being the bookkeeper and then club manager when Hank proposed; they place it around 1954-55.

segments.chapter: Marriage to Teddie and family
segments.title: Their anniversary and the approaching 50th
segments.summary: Jones and Teddie try to recall the wedding date, concluding summer 1955.

segments.chapter: Marriage to Teddie and family
segments.title: Their adopted daughter and the musical nephews
segments.summary: They adopted a daughter and raised two of Hank's sister's sons; nephews play piano, saxophone, drums and bass.

segments.chapter: Marriage to Teddie and family
segments.title: Matching family names and Teddie's birthplace near Charleston
segments.summary: Hank's father was Henry William and Teddie's William Henry; Teddie describes her father's role in a small South Carolina town.

segments.chapter: Marriage to Teddie and family
segments.title: Teddie's move to New York and the return visit to Charleston
segments.summary: Teddie, the ninth of ten children, was raised in New York by her older sister Beebe, and returned to South Carolina with Hank.

segments.chapter: Marriage to Teddie and family
segments.title: Teddie's father as long-serving mayor of her hometown
segments.summary: Her father was mayor for 33 years and the town confidant; the community has grown and land prices risen.

segments.chapter: Marriage to Teddie and family
segments.title: Wells' restaurant and Teddie keeping Hank's books
segments.summary: Teddie recalls Wells's ambitions and, with an accountant relative, kept Hank's books for years.

segments.chapter: Compositions, recording life and duets
segments.title: Thank Music and GG Grice returning Jones's compositions
segments.summary: Grice gave back copyrights of Jones's early tunes unasked, which went into Thank Music, a closed family corporation.

segments.chapter: Compositions, recording life and duets
segments.title: 'Teddie's Tune' and Tanaka's arrangement at Lincoln Center
segments.summary: Teddie's tune, which Hank wrote down and named; arranged by Japanese arranger Tanaka for a Lincoln Center concert.

segments.chapter: Compositions, recording life and duets
segments.title: Geoff Keezer's tribute record, and Ray Brown
segments.summary: Jones knew Keezer from Ray Brown's trio and recalls meeting Brown at 17 in Buffalo.

segments.chapter: Compositions, recording life and duets
segments.title: Buffalo's jazz scene and segregated musicians' unions
segments.summary: Major cities had separate black and white locals, including Detroit, Buffalo and Los Angeles.

segments.chapter: Compositions, recording life and duets
segments.title: GG Grice and the Donald Byrd jazz lab group; record dates with unknown labels
segments.summary: Jones was never in the lab group but recorded with Grice; recording names were often invented later, and musicians rarely knew who paid.

segments.chapter: Compositions, recording life and duets
segments.title: A&R man Teddy Reig and Teddie's memory
segments.summary: Jones recalls the heavy A&R man who worked for Savoy before Ozzie Cadena.

segments.chapter: Compositions, recording life and duets
segments.title: Rahsaan Roland Kirk and a pianist who played bass with his elbow
segments.summary: Jones was distracted by Kirk playing three horns on 'We Three Kings' and describes a Los Angeles pianist who played bass notes with an elbow.

segments.chapter: Compositions, recording life and duets
segments.title: Oscar Pettiford and what counts as avant-garde
segments.summary: The circle of recording musicians overlapped with Pettiford; Jones says yesterday's avant-garde becomes standard.

segments.chapter: Compositions, recording life and duets
segments.title: Feeling like an outsider, and the nonstop recording schedule
segments.summary: Jones felt outside the inner circle yet recorded constantly; Teddie fielded calls from A&R men and contractors.

segments.chapter: Compositions, recording life and duets
segments.title: Few recordings with his brothers: Thad's date with Mingus
segments.summary: Jones recorded with Thad and Elvin only twice, including a Debut date with Mingus.

segments.chapter: Compositions, recording life and duets
segments.title: 'Keeping Up with the Joneses' and Isham Jones
segments.summary: The Metro Jazz album of Thad and Isham Jones tunes was a marketing idea, likely Leonard Feather's; photo of the brothers.

segments.chapter: Compositions, recording life and duets
segments.title: The 'Elvin' session, Oliver Nelson and Art Davis
segments.summary: A 1961 Elvin Jones date with Frank Wess and Frank Foster, Oliver Nelson writing a tune minutes before the date, and bassist Art Davis.

segments.chapter: Compositions, recording life and duets
segments.title: The two Franks, Ernie Wilkins and the Basie arrangers
segments.summary: Jones links Frank Foster, Frank Wess and Ernie Wilkins from Detroit and Basie's band full of arrangers.

segments.chapter: Compositions, recording life and duets
segments.title: Savoy, Prestige and Riverside: pay at scale and albums in one day
segments.summary: Each label had its own A&R man but the business was handled the same way, at low scale, finishing an LP in a day at Van Gelder's.

segments.chapter: Compositions, recording life and duets
segments.title: A&R men Ozzie Cadena and Teddy Reig, sweetening dates, no rehearsals
segments.summary: Cadena and Reig understood the music; Jones also did sweetening dates; sessions had no rehearsals.

segments.chapter: Compositions, recording life and duets
segments.title: Orrin Keepnews, Galaxy and the duet with Tommy Flanagan
segments.summary: Jones did a one-day duet for Prestige/Fantasy while touring with Ella Fitzgerald, and a Galaxy solo album of spirituals.

segments.chapter: Compositions, recording life and duets
segments.title: Ken Burns's Jazz omitting the Lafayette Theater
segments.summary: Teddie and Hank feel the documentary did not go deep enough and left out the Lafayette Theater era.

segments.chapter: Compositions, recording life and duets
segments.title: The duo piano sessions with John Lewis
segments.summary: After choosing Steinways, Jones and Lewis worked from written arrangements, trading the roles of soloist and accompanist.

segments.chapter: Compositions, recording life and duets
segments.title: Flanagan duets versus Lewis, and four-piano dates
segments.summary: The Flanagan dates used head arrangements, the Lewis date charts; Jones did several four-piano records without great satisfaction.

segments.chapter: Compositions, recording life and duets
segments.title: Recording 'Sarala' with Cheick-Tidiane Seck's Malian musicians in Paris
segments.summary: Jones joined a Paris-based Malian band with no preparation and superimposed his playing on their music.

segments.chapter: Compositions, recording life and duets
segments.title: Declining to discuss a date with a mystic bandleader
segments.summary: Jones refuses comment on a record date with a mystic, saying only that the checks arrived on time.

segments.chapter: Lester Young, Broadway and the 1980s
segments.title: Lester Young: the most original person he met
segments.summary: Jones worked with Young at the Roundtable and in JATP and describes his entirely original talk, walk, clothes and playing.

segments.chapter: Lester Young, Broadway and the 1980s
segments.title: Lester Young's hipster language and the hidden-gin bus story
segments.summary: Jones could not follow Young, Granz and Jo Jones's slang; Shavers and Eldridge hid Young's gin on a JATP bus.

segments.chapter: Lester Young, Broadway and the 1980s
segments.title: Jo Jones: Lester's match and a versatile drummer
segments.summary: Jo Jones and Lester fit like hand in glove; Jones praises his range of styles and honesty.

segments.chapter: Lester Young, Broadway and the 1980s
segments.title: What makes a good show drummer: Jo Jones and Specs Powell
segments.summary: Show drummers must hold everything together and catch every act's cues, as Specs Powell did at CBS.

segments.chapter: Lester Young, Broadway and the 1980s
segments.title: Joining Broadway's 'Ain't Misbehavin'' through Luther Henderson
segments.summary: Henderson called him to do the Fats Waller revue; Jones took over from him after a few weeks and found the repeated exact playing tedious.

segments.chapter: Lester Young, Broadway and the 1980s
segments.title: Leaving the show after two years; subs who could not play stride
segments.summary: He tired of the show after about two years and the producers resisted his outside tours; his substitutes' stride was fake.

segments.chapter: Lester Young, Broadway and the 1980s
segments.title: How the show led to the Fats Waller recording
segments.summary: The show was background for singers, but Allard knew of it and picked Jones for the Waller record.

segments.chapter: Lester Young, Broadway and the 1980s
segments.title: A burst of 1978 recording dates in different styles
segments.summary: Watanabe, solo, Muse, Tommy Flanagan duo and Galaxy dates within weeks, fitted around Ella Fitzgerald's San Francisco engagement; Jones adjusts mentally to each.

segments.chapter: Lester Young, Broadway and the 1980s
segments.title: How the Sadao Watanabe date came about through East Wind
segments.summary: The Ito A&R men at East Wind, his first Japanese label, arranged it.

segments.chapter: Lester Young, Broadway and the 1980s
segments.title: Watanabe, Parker's tone, and Japanese players emulating Americans
segments.summary: Jones explains Watanabe's debt to Parker and Stitt, Parker's floating tone, and how he helped a musician working in another's idiom.

segments.chapter: Lester Young, Broadway and the 1980s
segments.title: Playing solo at Cafe Ziegfeld after the Broadway show
segments.summary: A late-night solo residency across the street gave him room to improvise and brought singers wanting to sit in.

segments.chapter: Lester Young, Broadway and the 1980s
segments.title: Touring Japan with Nancy Wilson and the Great Jazz Trio
segments.summary: Packaged Japanese tours with Wilson and the trio with Eddie Gomez and Jimmy Cobb.

segments.chapter: Lester Young, Broadway and the 1980s
segments.title: The violinist on 'Club New Yorker'
segments.summary: Jones recalls writing out solos for violinist Louis Eeley and learning of his death.

segments.chapter: Thad, recent work, outlook and advice
segments.title: The loss of Thad and Elvin Jones
segments.summary: Thad's death in 1986 and later Elvin's were great losses; Thad was recognized in his lifetime.

segments.chapter: Thad, recent work, outlook and advice
segments.title: Recording 'Upon Reflection', the Thad Jones tribute
segments.summary: The 1993 Verve record with George Mraz and Elvin Jones, a rubato 'A Child Is Born', and Jones says there is never closure after a brother's death.

segments.chapter: Thad, recent work, outlook and advice
segments.title: Missing the Chicago Jazz Festival Thad Jones reunion
segments.summary: A booking agent's error left Jones without an itinerary or tickets, so he missed the Chicago date and one in San Francisco.

segments.chapter: Thad, recent work, outlook and advice
segments.title: Recording with Joe Lovano
segments.summary: Jones enjoyed the ballad record with Lovano, George Mraz and Paul Motian and toured Europe with him.

segments.chapter: Thad, recent work, outlook and advice
segments.title: Upcoming tours, recordings and college seminars
segments.summary: Japanese and European tours, new recordings, and clinics at Michigan, Idaho, NYU and Harvard.

segments.chapter: Thad, recent work, outlook and advice
segments.title: Staying healthy on the road
segments.summary: Jones lives a regulated life, never drank or smoked, watches food and sleep, and takes medication to keep performing.

segments.chapter: Thad, recent work, outlook and advice
segments.title: Music as vocation and calling
segments.summary: Music began as a vocation and became a calling; his goal is to improve on his last performance.

segments.chapter: Thad, recent work, outlook and advice
segments.title: The state of jazz: encouraged by young players, wary of noise
segments.summary: Jones is encouraged that young people like jazz, but holds that music needs melody, rhythm and harmony.

segments.chapter: Thad, recent work, outlook and advice
segments.title: Five things to advance jazz
segments.summary: Setting an example, teaching, listening, supporting concerts and records, and more jazz on radio and TV.

segments.chapter: Thad, recent work, outlook and advice
segments.title: Advice to young musicians and close of the interview
segments.summary: Master the instrument and theory, avoid drugs, liquor and smoking, and stay healthy.
